question: Which of the following gases is released when baking soda reacts with vinegar?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Carbon dioxide**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• When baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) reacts with vinegar (acetic acid), **carbon dioxide (CO₂) gas is released**.
 
• The reaction is a classic example of an acid-base reaction, where acetic acid (acid) reacts with sodium bicarbonate (base).
 
• The chemical equation for the reaction is: **CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂**.
 
• The release of carbon dioxide is often observed as bubbling or fizzing during the reaction.
 
• This reaction is commonly used in baking to help dough rise, as the carbon dioxide gas creates air pockets in the dough.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Carbon monoxide:**

 
 
• Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless, and toxic gas formed by the incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels like coal, wood, or gasoline.
 
• It is not produced in the reaction between baking soda and vinegar.
 
• Exposure to carbon monoxide can cause serious health problems such as headaches, dizziness, and even death in high concentrations.
 
 
 
• **Ammonia:**
 
 
• Ammonia (NH₃) is a compound of nitrogen and hydrogen, commonly used in fertilizers, cleaning agents, and industrial applications.
 
• It has a pungent smell and is not involved in the reaction of baking soda and vinegar.
 
• Ammonia is produced industrially via the Haber process, which combines nitrogen and hydrogen gases under high pressure and temperature.
 
 
 
• **Hydrogen:**
 
 
• Hydrogen (H₂) is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe, commonly used as a fuel and in industrial processes.
 
• It is not produced in the reaction between baking soda and vinegar.
 
• Hydrogen gas is typically produced via processes such as electrolysis of water or steam methane reforming.
